transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-21
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE); Maria Santos (Coral CTO), David Chen (Head of ML), Leila Ahmed (PM)

---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really appreciate the time. I'm Jordan Lee with Redwood, AE on this account. Today Priya will walk through our model catalog, how we think about open models, the benchmark numbers and the compatibility matrices. We'll leave time for qa.

[00:28] Maria: Thanks Jordan, yeah we've been looking forward to this. Quick context - Coral's use case is clinical note summarization and an automated triage assistant. Privacy and latency are both pretty important for us.

[01:02] Priya: Great, thanks Maria. So quick agenda: catalog overview, picking models for high-quality summarization vs lightweight triage, benchmarks we typically see on common hardware, and then the compatibility matrix - what runs where and at what quantization. I'll also show Console screenshots for model selection and the Optimize suggestions.

[01:37] Ethan: I'll jump in on the console bits. There was a question about comparing variants and pinned versions, we'll show that.

[02:05] David: One ask up front — we mostly run prompts around 512 to 1k tokens input, and responses can be 200-800 tokens depending on the summarization length. Cost is a big driver for us, so any guidance on latency/cost tradeoffs is useful.

[02:40] Priya: Totally. Ok so first slide - model catalog: we surface curated open models with verified performance profiles. For each model we show per-token throughput numbers, typical latency at 1k and 2k context, and quality evals using a Redwood scoring harness. There are model families like LlamaX, Falcon variants, Mistral, and a set of quantization-friendly variants we verify. (note: sometimes model names get auto-transcribed - LlamaX might appear as "Llama ten")

[03:20] Jordan: To be clear, we also include compatibility matrices by hardware — e.g., A100/RTX6000/T4 or CPU-only, and we list recommended quantizations (int8, int4, nf4) and whether KV cache optimizations apply.

[04:01] Leila: How do you recommend choosing? We have a small set of clinical prompts and we care more about consistent quality than lowest cost for some flows.

[04:30] Priya: For that we'd typically pick a model higher on the quality curve — Mistral-XL or the LlamaX large variant are examples — and then use Optimize to suggest batching and caching to reduce cost. If you need deterministic outputs or high safety, we can recommend a tuned checkpoint. For triage, you could use a smaller Falcon-7B variant in quantized int8 or int4 to hit low-latency.

[05:10] Maria: Are there cases where quantization breaks clinical quality? We can't risk hallucinations in summaries.

[05:40] Priya: Good question — quantization can slightly change token probabilities, and with sensitive tasks like clinical summarization we recommend validating on a held-out prompt set. Our Optimize toolkit can run regression tests against your golden set and flag quality drops. For production we often keep higher-precision for summarization and use quantized variants for lower-risk queries.

[06:20] Jordan: We'll share the compatibility matrix spreadsheet — it maps model -> hardware -> quantization -> expected latency for 512/1k/2k contexts, and we annotate which models we've run clinical-style evals on.

[06:50] David: Can you walk through an example benchmark? Like Falcon-40B int8 on an A100 at 1k?

[07:12] Priya: Sure. So our benchmark sheet shows Falcon-40B int8 on a single A100 p4 gives ~180ms per 1k token chunk for generation-only throughput 1 request with KV cache cold, and ~110ms when KV warm for streaming responses. For LlamaX large at nf4 on A100 it's closer to 120-140ms cold and ~80ms warm. These are ballpark, will vary by prompt shape. We'll run your prompts to get precise numbers.

[08:05] Leila: Does Redwood validate tokenizer compatibility? We've had mismatch issues when switching model forks.

[08:28] Ethan: Yes — Console's model page surfaces tokenizer and vocabulary differences, and our model compatibility matrix flags any tokenization idiosyncrasies. We also have a quick CLI tool to check your prompts against the model tokenizer.

[09:00] Maria: On deployment modes — can you summarize differences between Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private for us? Security/regulatory is a factor.

[09:25] Jordan: Hosted is fastest to get started — API keys, rate limits, usage-based pricing. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and SLA-backed throughput which helps for steady production traffic. Private is the VPC/on-prem option with a customer-controlled control plane, KMS integration, and audit logs. For PHI-sensitive workloads many customers pick Private with HSM/KMS and network isolation.

[10:05] David: If we went Private, does Redwood still help with kernel selection and runtime tuning?

[10:25] Priya: Yes, the runtime is part of the package — we provide optimized kernels and a compatibility matrix that maps to supported hardware. For Private deployments we ship a control plane and we can help with benchmarking and kernel configuration. There's a bit more ops work on the customer side for on-prem, but we provide automation scripts.

[11:10] Leila: About model updates: how do you handle model version pinning and rollouts?

[11:30] Ethan: Console supports pinning model versions per route, can do canary rollouts, and automatic fallback policies to older variants if quality regresses. We tie this into our eval system so you can run regression tests on each candidate.
transcript_continued:
[12:05] Maria: Great. For our timeline - we want to run a short POC in Q1, ideally start benchmarks in December. For POC we want a small Dedicated pool or hosted sandbox?

[12:30] Jordan: For quick start we recommend Hosted sandbox for the first benchmarks, then move to Dedicated if throughput/cost make sense. Priya, can you outline what we'd need for the POC?

[12:48] Priya: Sure — we'll need sample prompts, typical traffic profile, desired SLOs for latency, and the golden evaluation set. We'll run per-model benchmarks and produce a recommendation (model + quantization + deployment).

[13:20] David: On security we need SOC2, SSO (SAML), audit logs retention policy, and KMS integration. Do you have docs?

[13:40] Jordan: Yes — I'll send the SOC2 summary, a SAML integration checklist, and the audit logs spec after the call. We support KMS/HSM integrations in Private and some Dedicated options.

[14:02] Leila: Any gotchas with cold starts when using smaller GPU pools? Our traffic is bursty.

[14:30] Priya: Cold starts happen if you scale to zero. For Dedicated we recommend a small baseline capacity to keep KV caches warm. We also support burst capacity configs to absorb spikes. Optimize can suggest autoscale thresholds based on your observed distribution.

[15:05] Ethan: I'll demo the Console — showing the catalog entry for Mistral-XL, the compatibility matrix view, and the Optimize suggestions for batching and prefix caching. (screen sharing noise)

[15:35] Ethan: Here you can see the model page — quality eval score, tokenizer notes, hardware compat. There's an "Estimate cost" button where you can input your prompt lengths and expected qps to get a monthly cost estimate.

[16:20] Maria: That estimate looks useful. Can it differentiate Hosted vs Dedicated pricing?

[16:40] Jordan: Yes, Console shows both hosted-per-token and a Dedicated estimate (amortized GPU + infra). We'll provide a more formal pricing spreadsheet in the next email.

[17:15] Priya: Quick note about regression testing — we link evals to specific routes. If an updated model fails a threshold we can auto-block rollout. This is how we prevent quality regressions.

[17:50] David: For the triage assistant, we'd prefer <200ms 95p latency. Is that realistic?

[18:10] Priya: For 200ms 95p you probably need a smaller model on beefy hardware or aggressive quantization, plus warmed KV cache. For that SLA consider Dedicated on A100 or H100, or a CPU+large mem config for smaller models. We'll run your flows to confirm.

[18:45] Maria: Any compliance evidence for healthcare customers you can share?

[19:05] Jordan: Yes, I'll include customer references and our compliance pack.

[19:30] Leila: What about tokenizer bleeding between model forks — we've had hallucination shifts after switching weights. Does Redwood track that?

[19:55] Ethan: We maintain per-model tokenizer notes and flag known incompatibilities. For any migration we recommend running the golden eval set.

[20:20] Priya: Ok last part — compatibility matrix example: for each model we list supported accelerators, max sequence length, recommended quantization, expected throughput at 512/1k, and whether KV optimizations are implemented. We'll share a CSV so you can filter by your target latency.

[21:05] Maria: Sounds good. Does the matrix indicate which models are verified on Private deployments too?

[21:25] Priya: Yes — we tag models as "Verified Hosted", "Verified Dedicated", or "Verified Private" based on internal testing. For Private we also note any additional kernel patches necessary.

[22:00] David: One operational question — how are model downloads and licensing handled for Private?

[22:20] Jordan: For open models we provide the artifacts and the install scripts. Licensing depends on model license — most open ones are fine but some forks have restrictions. We'll highlight that in the spreadsheet.

[23:00] Maria: Great, that's helpful. I think next steps are: send over the spreadsheets and security docs, run the benchmark on our prompts, and schedule the deep tech session.

[23:25] Jordan: Yep agreed. We'll follow up with the materials and get the benchmark queued. Thanks everyone.
